#10165. Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon

Edge AI complements the cloud to bring the best AI experiences. These rely on a continuous flow of context and intelligence across both, working as a model cascade where information is captured and processed in the right place at the right time. Ultra-low-power models on the edge can continuously sense and respond in real time, while seamlessly handing off to larger on-device or cloud models when deeper reasoning is needed.

Still, building for the edge is much harder than it should be. While cloud infrastructure has converged around a few standard software stacks, the edge is split across hundreds of proprietary chip architectures and incompatible toolchains. For ML developers, this creates a heavy fragmentation tax, where you end up rewriting kernels, re-quantizing models, and debugging vendor-specific compilers for every chip you target.

Last year, Google Research introduced Coral NPU with a simple idea: an open hardware and software standard is the only way to unify the edge and unlock developer productivity and portability. Our standards based, ML-first RISC-V architecture paired with a reliable open-source toolchain gives developers confidence that their models will compile and run, letting teams optimize a model once and deploy it across different SoC vendors, devices, and power envelopes.

Today, we are reaching three major milestones in the Coral effort:

Fixing fragmentation at the edge takes more than publishing an instruction set. Historically, many edge accelerators were designed to hit high peak-compute numbers on spec sheets, leaving compiler teams to figure out software support later. In practice, unsupported neural network layers fall back to a general-purpose CPU, which can hurt latency and drain the battery.

We designed the Coral NPU architecture and its compiler together from the start. Instead of chasing peak metrics, our focus is on energy-viable compute: helping to deliver the right performance at the right power envelope for your application.

Over the past year, we released the first three milestones of the 32-bit Coral NPU design: a C-programmable RISC-V scalar frontend for control flow (Milestone 1), an RVV v1.0 vector co-processor for SIMD operations (Milestone 2), and a tightly coupled memory subsystem with floating point support (Milestone 3). With this month's release of the Matrix Execution Unit (Milestone 4), the 32-bit architecture is complete.

Scalar and vector units are great for general control logic and signal processing, but modern ML workloads—from vision encoders to transformer attention layers—spend most of their time on 2D matrix-matrix (GEMM) and matrix-vector (GEMV) multiplication. Running 2D matrix math on a 1D vector engine forces the chip to repeatedly load weights and activations from memory, which can mean spending more energy moving data than doing math.

Our Matrix Execution Unit leverages the RISC-V VME specification (formally part of the Zvt family) to address this need and uses a dedicated outer-product multiply-accumulate (MAC) engine. Because an outer-product engine computes a full 2D tile of operations in a single cycle (256 MACs per cycle), it reuses weights and activations directly inside local registers. This brings quadratic throughput scaling to the core, configurable for up to 1 TOPS.

Having a dedicated matrix engine in a sub-10 mW envelope changes what developers can build on a small battery. Rather than stopping at simple keyword spotting or basic motion detection, devices can run continuous, multimodal workloads, including compact transformer models like Gemma, real-time voice translation on wearables, spatial audio filtering on hearables, and low-latency visual perception on robots.

To help silicon teams bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub.

To make the hardware easy to target without writing custom assembly, we are also releasing the v1.0 foundation of our open-source MLIR/IREE compiler toolchain.

With this stack, you can bring models from JAX, PyTorch, or TensorFlow through standard representations like StableHLO and TOSA. The compiler partitions workloads between the host CPU and the Coral NPU core, handles operator fusion, tiles matrices to fit local SRAM and matrix accumulators, and progressively lowers workloads directly to Coral NPU scalar, RVV v1.0 vector, and VME matrix instructions. Alongside our open-source MPACT simulator and reference FPGA design, hardware and software teams can benchmark models and tune silicon configurations before a chip ever goes to fabrication.

Turning an open standard into commercial silicon takes collaboration across the entire semiconductor value chain. To help silicon partners bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub, and we are partnering with VeriSilicon on the design implementation and verification (DV) to ensure turnkey readiness for silicon tape-outs. We are also working with GlobalFoundries on their 12LP+ FinFET process - accelerating core timing by 70%, and reducing standard-cell area by up to 15% across RTL iterations, with ongoing evaluation of 12LP+ ultra low-power libraries for the Matrix Execution Unit.

On the commercial silicon side, our collaboration with Synaptics shows how quickly this open standard translates into real hardware across very different power budgets without splitting the software experience.

At Synaptics Tech Day (October 20, 2026), Synaptics is launching three commercial silicon and hardware products built on Coral NPU technology and supported by the open IREE/MLIR toolchain:

Because both product families build on the same architecture and compiler foundation, ML teams can optimize a model once and deploy it to a milliwatt-class wearable (Coralboard SR) or a 1 TOPS board (Coralboard SL) using the same workflow. Developed in collaboration with hardware and System-on-Module partner Grinn, the Coralboard lineup also gives teams a direct path from devkit prototyping to commercial production hardware.

With our 32-bit architecture and v1.0 compiler stack in place, we are already working on the next phase of the roadmap, including a 64-bit Coral NPU architecture and CHERI support for security.

Whether you are designing a custom edge SoC, working on ML compilers, or deploying models to wearables and robotics, Coral NPU can help give you an open path from model to silicon. Here is where you can get started:

#10163. Oppo reportedly cancels Find X10 Ultra thanks to RAMageddon

The Oppo Find X9 Ultra was my favorite new phone of 2026 but, thanks to RAMageddon, the company is apparently canceling its sequel.

Leaker Digital Chat Station reports on Weibo in a slightly cryptic post that, apparently, Oppo has canceled plans to release a Find X10 Ultra. The reason isn’t mentioned directly, but RAMageddon is almost certainly the reason. With skyrocketing prices, Ultra phones have been on the chopping block for a lot of Android brands, as specs like 16GB of RAM become harder to sustain at an acceptable price point.

The Oppo Find X9 Ultra packed a top-tier Snapdragon chip and 16GB of RAM, where Oppo’s current Find X10 Pro Max uses a MediaTek flagship instead and 12GB of RAM in most variants, and that one is already very expensive in markets such as Europe.

Find X10 Ultra was expected to offer, in part, a 200MP 1/1.12-inch main sensor with LOFIC, a 200MP periscope telephoto with 1/1.3-inch sensor, a 50MP 10x periscope telephoto, and a 100MP front-facing square sensor camera. In other words, an absolute camera powerhouse, and now it’s dead.

#10161. Google Messages homepage redesign: Pinned chat avatars, bottom search, corner Gemini

In addition to the new app icon, Google Messages for Android is testing a big homepage redesign that has three core components.

Update 11/7: Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.

This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s currently just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.

You’ll see large contact photos appear above all chats, which pushes the list of other conversations down the page. Like iMessage on iOS, this layout has the downside of not showing any history or last sent information.

Meanwhile, Google is testing another change where search becomes a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside new chat. When you’re scrolling down the page, you’ll see “Search” in a pill-shaped button, with the other button minimized.

Hate the idea of just the pinned "bobble head" look. I like being able to view message tidbits. Plus, it's directly copying Apple (enough said). I have to use an iPhone at my job. I hate the pinned bubble conversation look and more importantly it's function.

Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive, while boosting one-handed usability.

Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image. This matches the design leveraged by Workspace apps on desktop and mobile.

These updates are currently in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to all testers. Some users have all aspects of the redesign, but it appears that Google is rolling out the various components in a piecemeal fashion.

#10159. Android tablets are back, but are they for you?

Android tablets have always been a bit of a touchy subject, but it’s abundantly clear that the form factor is making a comeback. But, as someone who’s a fan of the smaller sizes, are you actually using the gargantuan Android tablets that every company seems obsessed with? In other words – are you the customer for the Android tablets these brands are selling?

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

For a while there, Android tablets had hit what felt like a dead end. Bigger smartphones and cooling of the tablet market as a whole, along with the general sentiment that Apple was doing a way better job with the iPad anyway, left the category in a place that felt stagnant – and that’s the nice way of putting it.

But, over the past few years, Android tablets have had a renaissance.

New form factors, big releases from a variety of brands, and flagship-tier devices left and right. Despite Android’s push into foldables and still-huge displays on nearly every smartphone, tablets are very much back. Prior to RAMageddon’s worst impacts, tablet sales were growing for nearly everyone, and Android brands were seeing a larger slice of the pie.

Anyway, this is on my mind right now because I’ve had a lot of Android tablets arrive in my office in the past few weeks, capping off a lot of tablet announcements in the past few months. I just finished up with Redmagic Astra 2, a tablet I think fits the description of “Android’s iPad Mini OLED,” and I’m in the process of moving into tablets from Lenovo and Amazon. Our Jordan Floyd has also been testing out the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra behind the scenes. And if there’s one trend amongst recent tablet releases, it’s that big tablets seem to be the primary focus among a lot of brands.

Take Amazon’s new Google Play-equipped Alexa Tablet lineup, for example.

The Alexa Tablet 12 is the crown jewel of the lineup, packing the most powerful specs and a premium anti-glare display. It’s the only one that gets a “Pro” moniker, while the 11-inch and 8-inch models are noticeable steps down. Unboxing the Alexa Tablet 8 this week, for example, I was immediately reminded this is not a premium device – the screen makes that clear without any hesitation whatsoever. It was a case of whiplash after setting up the Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 with its 4K display.

It’s a weird one for me. I’ve never been a big fan of these super-sized Android tablets (or iPads, for that matter). I can get behind a 10-inch or 11-inch model, but I find myself more at home on the smaller slates. They’re fantastic for travel as an alternative to draining my phone’s battery, while I find myself just reaching for a laptop instead if I want a bigger screen. A big tablet, regardless of specs, can rarely replace a proper laptop for me, so lugging both around just sounds like more trouble than it’s worth.

But, clearly, people are buying these bigger slates. Samsung appears to be seeing enough success with its mammoth Galaxy Tab S Ultra lineup to keep the 14.6-inch tablet around each year while the smaller sizes are now on an every-other-year cycle. Lenovo’s lineup is virtually all underpowered when the screen size goes down, aside from the Legion Tab that’s now $900.

Are you buying these bigger tablets? What are you using them for?

I imagine that most folks opting for a bigger tablet are using these in the place of a laptop. Thinner and lighter, longer battery life, etc. And in cases like the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its $550~ price tag, I get the appeal. Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 takes that down a notch for me at $799 – you’re getting into laptop territory there – but it still is a compelling-enough alternative if it fits your needs. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra at $1,400 plus a $200 keyboard, yeah I don’t get that one at all.

Let’s discuss! I want to know if you’re using an Android tablet, what you’re using it for, and what size you actually prefer.

Ladies and gents, we’ve finally got a new flagship in the US. Motorola Signature 27 is launching on November 19 and looks excellent, though its flashy spec sheet won’t come cheap at $1,599.

Finally, something good came out of Googlebook

Googlebook is a disaster, but there’s finally one good thing coming out of it in Henry Cavill’s new “Mustache Protocol” game which, supposedly, was built on Googlebook. I’ll bite my tongue there, but the accompanying video brought a needed bit of joy into my week.

#10158. Best Static Website Hosting Providers in 2027: Free and Paid Options Compared

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You've finished building your website. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are ready, everything works locally, and now you need somewhere to publish it.

Static website hosting is one of the simplest ways to get a website online. Many providers offer free plans, and you don't need to maintain a traditional web server.

The harder part is choosing the right provider. Some let you upload a single HTML file and share it immediately. Others connect to GitHub, automatically deploy code changes, and support entire development teams.

We've compared eight static hosting providers, including TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and GitHub Pages. Below, you'll find their free hosting limits, pricing, advantages, and drawbacks, along with recommendations for different types of projects.

Static website hosting is a service that stores and delivers pre-built website files, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts.

Unlike traditional server-rendered websites, static sites don't need a server to generate each page when someone visits. The HTML is already prepared and can be delivered directly to the visitor's browser.

That doesn't mean static websites can't be interactive. JavaScript can still handle navigation, forms, filtering, and other features. Static sites can also communicate with external APIs or databases.

The main distinction is how pages are generated.

You can write a static website using plain HTML or generate one with frameworks and tools such as Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, or Next.js static export.

Static hosting is also commonly associated with Jamstack, an approach that separates the front end from back-end services.

Lower hosting costs: Many providers let you publish smaller websites for free.

Simpler maintenance: There's no application server or server-side runtime to maintain for the static pages themselves.

Efficient content delivery: Static files can be cached across a content delivery network (CDN), reducing the distance between visitors and website assets.

There are limitations, too. If your website requires user authentication, database operations, or server-side functionality, you'll need additional services or a hosting platform that supports them.

We compared eight providers based on their deployment methods, free plan allowances, pricing, and suitability for different projects.

Free hosting limits: Bandwidth, storage, build allowances, and restrictions.

Deployment process: Whether you can upload files directly or need a Git repository.

Custom domains and HTTPS: Support for publishing under your own domain.

Development features: Automatic deployments, preview environments, and integrations.

Pricing: What happens when a project exceeds its free allowance.

Usage restrictions: Whether free hosting is suitable for commercial projects.

The following table summarizes the main differences between all eight services.

Free plans aren't directly comparable. For example, Vercel restricts its Hobby plan to personal, non-commercial use, while GitHub Pages prohibits using the service as free hosting for an online business or commercial SaaS.

Bandwidth limits also aren't the same as visitor limits. A website serving large images or downloadable files can consume its monthly allowance with relatively few visitors.

Cloudflare Pages is a strong choice for developers who want to host static websites without worrying about a conventional monthly bandwidth cap.

You can connect a GitHub or GitLab repository, and Cloudflare automatically builds and deploys the website when you push changes. Direct uploads are also supported.

A maximum individual file size of 25 MiB.

The combination is useful for blogs, documentation websites, and other projects that primarily serve HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images.

Cloudflare also provides preview deployments, custom domains, and HTTPS support.

No fixed bandwidth cap for static asset delivery.

Generous free plan for typical static websites.

Monthly build limits can matter for frequently updated projects.

Cloudflare's product range can make the initial setup less straightforward for beginners.

Cloudflare is increasingly emphasizing Workers Static Assets for new projects. Pages remains available, but developers starting a new application should compare both deployment approaches.

For a conventional static website, however, Pages is still a practical option, particularly when traffic could grow beyond the limits of other free plans.

See the official Cloudflare Pages limits for the current allowances.

Netlify combines static website hosting with tools designed to make development and deployment easier.

Connect a Git repository, configure your build settings, and Netlify can publish a new version whenever you push changes.

It also creates deploy previews, allowing you to inspect changes before merging them into your production branch.

This is useful when multiple people work on the same website or when you want to review design changes before publishing.

Netlify supports custom domains, HTTPS, serverless functions, and form handling.

Netlify's free plan uses a credit-based model with 300 credits per month.

Production deployments consume 15 credits each.

Web requests consume 2 credits per 10,000 requests.

Deploy previews and branch deployments consume no deployment credits.

The paid Personal plan starts at $9 per month and includes 1,000 monthly credits.

Convenient Git integration and deploy previews.

Built-in features such as forms and serverless functions.

Suitable for both simple websites and more advanced front-end projects.

Credit-based pricing requires monitoring several types of usage.

A busy site with frequent deployments can consume its free allowance faster than expected.

When comparing Netlify alternatives, Cloudflare Pages is particularly worth considering if your main concern is bandwidth.

For developers choosing between Vercel vs Netlify, the deciding factor is often the framework and workflow. Netlify offers a flexible approach to static site deployment, while Vercel has particularly close integration with Next.js.

Vercel is particularly well suited to Next.js applications, although it also supports React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, and other frameworks.

Like Netlify, Vercel connects to your Git repository and deploys updates automatically.

Every deployment receives its own URL, which helps developers review changes before publishing them to the main website.

Vercel also supports server-side rendering, functions, and other features beyond traditional static site hosting.

There is one important restriction: Vercel Hobby is intended for personal, non-commercial use only.

If you're deploying a business website or another commercial project, you'll need an appropriate paid plan.

Convenient deployment workflow for Next.js.

Supports both static and server-rendered applications.

Paid usage can involve multiple resource-based charges.

If you're building a personal Next.js application, Vercel is an obvious candidate. For a basic HTML website, however, its additional framework features may be unnecessary.

GitHub Pages is a straightforward way to publish a website directly from a GitHub repository.

It works particularly well for developer portfolios, project documentation, open-source websites, and small informational sites.

You can upload HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files to a repository, configure GitHub Pages, and publish them under a github.io subdomain.

GitHub Pages can serve existing static files or build websites using supported workflows, including Jekyll and GitHub Actions.

Published websites have a maximum size of 1 GB.

Bandwidth has a soft limit of 100 GB per month.

Free accounts can publish Pages sites from public repositories.

The bandwidth and build restrictions are soft limits, meaning they aren't necessarily enforced as strict cutoffs.

Simple integration with GitHub repositories.

Well suited to documentation and open-source projects.

Free accounts require a public repository for Pages.

GitHub Pages is not intended for running online businesses, e-commerce websites, or commercial SaaS products.

GitHub Pages is particularly convenient if your code already lives on GitHub and you only need to publish documentation or a portfolio.

For commercial websites, Cloudflare Pages or Netlify may be more appropriate.

The GitHub Pages documentation explains its hosting limits and usage restrictions.

Not every website needs a repository, deployment pipeline, or command-line interface.

If you've created a simple HTML page and want to share it, TiinyHost lets you upload an HTML file or ZIP archive and publish it under a shareable URL.

It can also host PDFs, making it useful for sharing documents and presentations alongside website projects.

The main advantage is the upload process. You don't need to configure a repository or install development tools before publishing.

Sharing an HTML file with someone who doesn't use Git.

The free plan includes one active site, a 3 MB project upload limit, and an allowance of 5,000 monthly visits.

The Tiny plan costs €5 per month when billed monthly. It supports uploads up to 25 MB and includes built-in analytics.

The Solo plan starts at €13 per month when billed monthly and adds features such as custom domains, password protection, and additional projects.

Annual billing is available at lower effective monthly prices.

No Git repository or command line required.

Suitable for previews and smaller projects.

The free plan's 3 MB limit is restrictive for websites with many images or other assets.

Custom domains require the Solo plan or higher.

Upload-based publishing is less convenient than Git automation for frequently updated websites.

For someone who simply needs free HTML hosting to share a small project, TiinyHost is worth considering.

For a larger production website that receives regular updates, Git-based hosting is likely to be more manageable.

Firebase Hosting is Google's hosting service for static websites and web application assets.

It integrates with other Firebase products, including Authentication, Cloud Firestore, and Cloud Functions.

That makes it useful when a website needs static hosting but also relies on Google's back-end services.

Deployment is handled through the Firebase command-line interface.

After configuring your project, you can deploy using:

Firebase distributes website assets through its CDN and supports custom domains with SSL certificates.

The Blaze plan uses pay-as-you-go billing while retaining applicable no-cost allowances.

One detail worth checking is the distinction between Firebase Hosting and Firebase App Hosting. They are separate products with different features and pricing models.

Integrates with Firebase Authentication and Firestore.

Useful for applications already using Google's developer services.

Initial setup is more involved than uploading an HTML file.

The daily transfer allowance may become restrictive for larger websites.

Firebase Hosting makes the most sense when Firebase is already part of your application.

For a standalone static blog or portfolio that doesn't use Firebase services, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages may be simpler.

Amazon S3 and CloudFront offer a different approach to static hosting.

Instead of using a platform that handles the entire deployment process, you combine AWS services to store and deliver your website.

S3 stores the website files, while CloudFront distributes them through a CDN.

This setup provides control over caching, permissions, security, and integration with other AWS services.

It can be suitable for organizations already using AWS or developers who need specific infrastructure configurations.

AWS uses usage-based pricing for S3 storage, requests, and applicable CloudFront usage.

Free allowances may apply depending on your account and the current AWS pricing program, but you should calculate costs based on your expected traffic, storage, and requests.

Unlike simpler hosting services, there isn't one fixed monthly price for every website.

Several services can contribute to the final bill.

Incorrect permissions or origin settings can cause access errors.

One common issue when setting up S3 static website hosting is receiving a 403 Forbidden error because of bucket permissions or CloudFront origin configuration.

AWS recommends using CloudFront Origin Access Control with a regular S3 bucket origin so that the bucket can remain private. This differs from exposing the S3 website endpoint directly, which does not support HTTPS on its own.

AWS S3 and CloudFront are worth considering if you need that level of control. For a small static website, a managed hosting platform usually requires less setup.

Render is a cloud platform that supports static websites alongside web services, databases, background workers, and other application components.

Its static hosting works through a Git repository.

Connect your repository, select the build command and publish directory, and Render automatically deploys your website.

The service includes CDN delivery, custom domains, and managed TLS certificates.

Render is particularly useful when your project includes both a static front end and back-end services that you want to manage through the same platform.

Render's Hobby workspace is free and includes:

500 standard build pipeline minutes per month.

Additional bandwidth is billed at $0.15 per GB under the current pricing structure, so the Hobby workspace should not be treated as unlimited free hosting.

The Pro workspace costs $25 per month, excluding any applicable usage-based compute charges.

Static websites and back-end services on one platform.

The 5 GB included bandwidth allowance is relatively small.

Render makes sense when you're already using it for other parts of an application.

If you only need to host a static HTML website, Cloudflare Pages offers a more generous bandwidth allowance without the additional platform complexity.

Free static website hosting can be sufficient for a personal portfolio, documentation site, prototype, or small informational website.

However, the restrictions vary considerably between providers.

Some hosts measure data transfer, while others use visitor counts or a credit system. Check how each provider calculates usage rather than comparing headline numbers alone.

If your website rebuilds whenever you publish content, deployment limits matter. A blog updated a few times a month has different requirements from an application receiving dozens of deployments every day.

Free hosting doesn't always mean you can run a business website. Vercel's Hobby plan and GitHub Pages have restrictions that may rule out certain commercial projects.

Some services include custom domains on free plans. Others require an upgrade before you can connect one.

A free plan might stop serving additional usage, while another provider may bill for overages.

Before publishing a production website, check the provider's billing behavior and configure spending controls where available.

The right service depends primarily on how you build your website and what you intend to do with it.

For most developers publishing a conventional static website, Cloudflare Pages is a reasonable starting point.

If you're working with Git and want convenient previews and deployment tools, Netlify is another good choice.

For small files, temporary demos, and client previews, a simpler upload-based service may save time.

You should also consider how often the website will change.

Uploading files manually may be fine for a page that rarely changes. For a website with regular content updates, automated deployments from Git will generally be easier to maintain.

Publishing your website is only the first step. If you want search engines to discover and understand your pages, check the technical SEO basics before sharing the URL.

Every important page should have a descriptive HTML title and a relevant meta description.

You can use the Meta Tags Generator to create the necessary markup.

Open Graph tags help control how a page appears when shared on platforms that support them.

Set the title, description, canonical page URL where appropriate, and preview image.

A robots.txt file tells compliant crawlers which paths they may access. It doesn't guarantee indexing or prevent a public page from appearing in search results.

Use the Robots.txt Generator to create your crawler rules.

Include a sitemap with the canonical URLs you want search engines to discover.

Structured data helps search engines interpret eligible content.

Depending on the website, you may want Organization, Article, BreadcrumbList, or other relevant schema types.

The JSON-LD Schema Generator can help generate markup.

Confirm the correct domain loads over HTTPS.

Check canonical tags and redirect behavior.

Make sure important pages don't contain unintended noindex directives.

Test page performance and Core Web Vitals.

Verify the website in Google Search Console.

Static hosting makes serving website files relatively straightforward, but technical SEO still requires configuration and testing.

Cloudflare Pages is a good general-purpose choice because of its free static asset bandwidth and Git integration. Netlify is well suited to teams that need deploy previews, while GitHub Pages works well for portfolios and documentation. The best option depends on your deployment workflow, traffic requirements, and whether the website is commercial.

Yes. TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Firebase Hosting, Render, and several other services offer free hosting options. Most free plans have restrictions involving bandwidth, deployments, storage, or usage. Check the terms before using a free plan for a business website.

A small static website can cost nothing to host if it stays within a provider's free allowances. Paid plans vary from fixed monthly subscriptions to usage-based pricing. Domain registration, paid back-end services, and additional storage or bandwidth may increase the total cost.

For a standalone HTML file, upload-based hosting is generally the simplest approach. Services such as TiinyHost let you publish a file without configuring Git or a build process. If the project already lives in a GitHub repository, GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages may be more convenient.

GitHub Pages is a sensible option for documentation, open-source projects, and personal portfolios. Netlify offers more deployment features, including preview environments, forms, and functions. It also supports commercial projects, making it more appropriate for some business websites that would fall outside GitHub Pages' permitted uses.

Static website hosting doesn't need to be expensive or complicated. The important part is choosing a service that matches your website and deployment process.

Cloudflare Pages is a good starting point for static websites that need generous free bandwidth. Netlify is useful for Git-based development, while GitHub Pages suits personal projects and documentation.

If you're publishing a small HTML file or sharing a prototype, upload-based hosting may be all you need.

#10153. A Practical Introduction to the Twitch Helix API

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Behind almost every Twitch tool you have ever seen, the stat trackers, the moderation bots, the stream overlays, the alert systems, sits one interface: the Twitch Helix API. Twitch is unusually generous with public data, and Helix is the door to it. If you have ever wondered how third-party sites know who is live, what a channel's viewership looks like, or details a Twitch profile page does not even display, this is the machinery.

This article is a practical overview of Helix for developers who have not used it yet: what it offers, how its authentication works, what people build with it, and where the sharp edges are.

Helix is Twitch's current REST API, served from api.twitch.tv/helix. It replaced the old "Kraken" API, which was fully retired in 2022, so any tutorial still showing Kraken endpoints is a sign to keep scrolling. Helix covers users, streams, channels, games and categories, clips, chat, moderation actions, subscriptions, and events, with JSON in and JSON out.

Two things distinguish it from many platform APIs. First, a large share of it works without any user's permission, because the data is public by Twitch's own definition. Second, it is paired with EventSub, a push system that notifies your application when things happen (a stream goes live, a user follows, a message arrives) instead of forcing you to poll. Most serious Twitch tools use both: Helix for lookups, EventSub for live events.

Authentication is where most newcomers stall, mainly because Twitch offers several OAuth flows and tutorials rarely say which one you actually need. The short version:

Every request needs a Client ID, which you get by registering an application in the Twitch developer console (two-factor authentication on your account is required first). Requests carry the Client ID and a bearer token together; forgetting the Client ID header is the classic mystery 401.

App access tokens come from the client credentials flow, a single server-to-server request with your ID and secret. They have no user attached and that is fine, because public reads, user profiles, live streams, top games, clips, need no user context. For most read-only tools, this is the only flow you ever touch.

Tokens expire, so real applications cache them with their reported lifetime and refresh on a 401 rather than assuming a token lives forever.

A tour of the endpoints that power most tools:

Users. Give the users endpoint a username and it returns the account's public record: display name, profile image, description, Affiliate or Partner status, and the account's exact creation timestamp. That last field is interesting because Twitch does not display it anywhere on a profile, yet it is one of the platform's most useful trust signals, moderators use account age to spot throwaway accounts, and streamers use it to filter giveaway entries. The creation date alone powers a small subcategory of tools: free account age checkers, such as Twitch account age checker, are essentially this one endpoint with a clean page around it, taking any public username and returning the creation date, age, avatar, and broadcaster status. It is a good illustration of how far a single well-chosen Helix field can go.

Streams. The stream's endpoint reports who is live right now, with titles, categories, thumbnail URLs, and viewer counts. This is the backbone of every "is my favorite streamer live" notifier and every directory-style site, and polling it over time is how stat trackers chart viewership history.

Games and categories. Top games, category search, and metadata. Combined with streams data, this is how analytics sites rank categories and how tools answer "how crowded is this category right now."

Clips and videos. Clip metadata, view counts, and creation tools. Highlight compilers and clip-sharing bots live here.

Helix enforces a points-based rate limit per Client ID, and every response tells you where you stand through Ratelimit-Limit, Ratelimit-Remaining, and Ratelimit-Reset headers. Well-behaved tools read those headers and back off before hitting zero; badly behaved ones retry 429s in a loop and wonder why things get worse. For lookup-style tools the practical fix is caching, data like account creation dates never changes, so there is no reason to ask twice.

A few more edges worth knowing before they bite:

Usernames change, IDs do not. Store user IDs, not logins, or your saved data will eventually point at the wrong person.

Missing users are not errors. Looking up a nonexistent username returns a successful response with an empty data array, so handle the empty case explicitly.

Batching exists. The users endpoint takes up to 100 logins in one call, which matters the moment your tool checks lists instead of individuals.

Secrets stay server-side. The client secret identifies your application; calling the token endpoint from browser code hands your app's identity to anyone who opens devtools. Public-facing tools put a small server between the browser and Twitch.

The reason Twitch's third-party ecosystem is so large is that the barrier is so low: one public API, generous free access, and a platform where small questions genuinely matter to people. That is why the space is full of narrow tools that each answer one thing well, when was this account created, is this channel live, how fast is this category growing, which clips popped this week. Most of them are a weekend of work on top of one or two endpoints, and some of them grow into real products.

If you want to start, the path is short: register an application at the developer console, request an app access token, and call the users or streams endpoint for something you actually care about. The official documentation at dev.twitch.tv is current and well maintained, which is not something every platform can claim. Pick one piece of data Twitch collects but does not display, put a clean interface on it, and you are following the same recipe as most of the Twitch tools you already use.

#10150. Resolved: CSS Class Prefix Selector

Just looking at what Bramus shared the other day:

First off, if you don’t follow Bramus, where have you been?! Jokes aside, his job is to be first-in-line on new features like this — especially as it pertains to Chrome — so it’s worth keeping tabs on his RSS and/or social.

It’s not a new proposal. Lea posted it back in 2024 and has advocated for it the whole while. As Bramus mentions in his post, what’s new is that the proposal was formally adopted and, as of three days ago, it has been added to the Selectors Level 5 spec draft. So, chances are that we’ll see it formally adopted at some point and implemented somewhere even sooner.

I really like the ergonomics of it. Existing substring selectors — class^="prefix" and class=*" prefix" — are verbose and defintely less readable than a simple .prefix-*.

And it’s not like [data-attribute] selectors that require not only an extra step touching HTML but still added verbosity.

But something makes me wince at the idea. I can’t quite put my finger on it. Perhaps it’s redundancy as in, we can already do this with existing selectors? Bramus cites performance issues with existing substring selectors as a primary reason we need this. But Brian Kardell’s reply resonates with me:

Yeah, I guess if we have a very specific case we can optimize it more than a general one, but I'm not seeing how this is a lot more specific than the version above which almost exists today. Feels like if we could optimize this we could optimize that. I'd be curious how it is optimized.

Then again, I do like how we extended color functions for brevity, like:

And it’s backwards-compatible, so no real harm if you continue to use the “old” way. It’s not like substring selectors don’t have other use cases and become totally obsolete. But maybe that’s it: this isn’t an “upgrade” of something we already have, but a new thing that isn’t progressive enhancement out of the gate. We’d have to @support it until it becomes a Baseline feature:

…which may or may not be a long wait. But we don’t know. And if ergonomics are the selling point, then we’re losing that in the wait.

Should also note that the wildcard doesn’t match other conditions or non-dashed cases:

Another worthy note is that the spec currently implies (but doesn’t explicitly state) that this has the same specificity as a class selector, (0,1,0). That’d make sense, as .prefix-* is really no different than writing .prefix-variation.

That said, I like how it might possibly look in a nested syntax:

…and Dave’s plea to support selecting web components:

Maybe I just convinced myself that I like it. Again, I dunno. Just take the added convenience and move on! Yada yada.

Only supporting it as a dashed prefix is kind of weird. I do like it as replacing attribe-starts-with, since for that to work it needs to be the first class of potentially multiple.

color: rgb(10, 20, 20 / .25) is invalid. The new syntax has spaces between the RGB components.

Furthermore, rgb(10 20 20) is different from rgb(10% 20% 20%).

The first one, rgb(10 20 20), is equivalent to #0a1414 or rgb(3.92% 7.84% 7.84%), a very dark seagreen. That is because numbers with no % in RGB are in the [0, 255] interval (so the % equivalent is 10/255*100%, 20/255*100%…).

The second one, rgb(10% 20% 20%) is equivalent to #1a3333 or rgb(26 51 51), some kind of seagreen, visibly lighter than the first.

#10148. WordPress PHP-Only Block Registration

You want to build a custom WordPress block. But you don’t want to learn React, manage a build pipeline, or deal with NPM packages.

Seven and half years after blocks arrived in Core, WordPress introduces a way to build blocks without any of these things. All you need is PHP.

A traditional WordPress block needs to be registered twice. Once in PHP, and once in JavaScript.

But WordPress 7.0 introduces a new and streamlined approach, allowing you to register a block using only PHP.

Let’s use this feature to build a Hello World Block:

The block is fully functional in the block editor, and fits right in with all the other blocks:

The key addition is the 'autoRegister' => true flag in the supports section. When set, WordPress automatically generates the required JavaScript for your block based on the PHP registration. This includes the client-side registration, and the editor preview.

Attributes let users customize the block’s appearance and behavior. In traditional block development you not only need to define the attributes, but also build out the corresponding controls in the editor interface.

With PHP-only registration, all that is needed is the attributes definition during block registration:

This code registers a greeting attribute as a string, with a default value. WordPress generates the corresponding input control in the block’s Settings sidebar.

At first sight, there is a lot to like about PHP-only registered blocks. For any WordPress developer, it feels like the good old times when programming was simpler.

You might be tempted to delay learning JavaScript block development indefinitely. But the PHP-only approach has important limitations worth understanding.

The editor displays the HTML as returned by the block’s render_callback PHP function. When the block is first displayed or when the user interacts with one of its controls, the editor component requests a new PHP render from a REST API endpoint.

While blocks rendered this way integrate seamlessly into the editor, they are not part of the single page JavaScript application that powers the entire editor experience.

First, you cannot add any controls within the block preview. This means you are limited to the auto-generated controls in the Settings sidebar.

The default interaction mode with blocks is the block preview itself. Imagine that you need a testimonial block. With a JavaScript rendered block, you would build out the testimonial design, and allow editing in place.

With a PHP-rendered block you can only use the sidebar. And even here you are limited, as currently there’s no support for image uploads or multiline text.

With JavaScript, you can allow editing in the block, as well as in the sidebar. Additionally you have access to all the controls that WordPress Core uses, and can even implement your own.

But without JavaScript, you’ll always be limited to the options WordPress provides based on the registered attributes of your PHP-only block.

Secondly you cannot attach any JavaScript to markup in the block preview. Imagine you want to develop a block that pulls five related posts, and which displays them in a slider. For that you would output the markup, and then pass a DOM node to the JavaScript library which then transforms the raw markup into the desired slider interface.

This reliance on finding and manipulating DOM elements is typical for traditional JavaScript development. But with PHP-only registered blocks in the block editor, the markup is fetched asynchronously and replaced on every re-render. This makes interacting with the DOM of the block preview unreliable or impossible.

While the front end render works fine with JavaScript libraries, the editor authoring experience will not work correctly. Even if you manage to attach any event listeners on first load, these will be disconnected the moment the preview re-renders.

These limitations are caused by the architecture of this feature, and they will not change in the future.

On the initial load of the block editor, WordPress loads the post data from the database into a client-side store managed by JavaScript. Any changes that you make in the editor update this data store on the client side. But the database isn’t updated until you save the post.

PHP-only registered blocks bypass this client-side store. When a block renders, it queries the database directly. But the database might contain stale data compared to what’s currently in the editor. Even worse, the PHP-rendered block isn’t notified of changes in the client side data, so it can’t refresh when data changes.

Let’s take a practical example: Imagine you are building a block that displays a header element with the post title. When the user changes the title in the editor, your block will still show the value from the database. You would need to save the post and reload the editor for the changed title to show up in the PHP-only block.

This makes PHP-only blocks unsuitable for any block that displays data that the user can change in the editor like title, content, excerpt, features images, or attached terms.

PHP-only registered blocks render through a REST API endpoint. So the same code renders the editor preview and the front end. But there is a critical difference: the global state.

On the front end, blocks render within The Loop, which sets key global variables like $post. Template tags like the_title() or the_content() rely on these globals to know which post is displayed.

But REST APIs are stateless, and don’t rely on global state. The endpoint that renders the block editor preview accepts a post ID parameter, but the editor component does not pass it through. This means that your render callback has no way to know which post is edited.

This limits the functions that you can use in the block editor preview. Template tags or functions like get_post_meta() need to know about the post context.

This is a significant architectural limitation as of WordPress 7.0. This could be addressed by passing the post ID to the endpoint, but there are no concrete plans to change this at the time of this writing.

WordPress 7.0 supports only three attribute types: strings, numbers, and booleans. These map to four basic editor controls: text inputs, number inputs, checkboxes, and a dropdown.

This screenshot shows a block that uses all available user interface elements:

The dropdown element is the only advanced control, but it has a significant limitation: it does not support keyed arrays. This makes it impossible to have a label that differs from the stored value.

Let’s take the example of a related posts block where users can select a category. You want to display the category names in the dropdown, but store the category IDs. This isn’t possible.

Instead, you must choose between displaying names or slugs, which both are user-editable, and store that value:

Using slugs not only doesn’t look good in the interface, but this implementation will also break when renaming a category. All existing blocks referencing the old slug will not be able to pull the related posts. IDs are stabler, and would only be invalid when the category is deleted.

Beyond dropdowns, essential controls — like image uploads, rich text editors, or date pickers — are absent. This might change in future releases, but again, there are no plans for it as of yet.

It’s easy to get discouraged looking at these limitations. It is true that PHP-only registered blocks are a poor choice for building new blocks from scratch.

But I consider them to still be very valuable because there is one use case where these limitations do not matter: migrating legacy PHP code into block themes. This WordPress 7.0 feature is a real game changer when it comes to developers adopting block themes, which is still a barrier of sorts for many theme authors.

In my experience, block themes are more performant, easier to maintain, and faster to build than legacy themes. Yet many developers are still relying on classic themes. And that is not by choice, but because of existing PHP-based features.

Until now, migrating these features came up against nearly insurmountable barriers. First, the need to learn JavaScript block development, and set up an entirely new development workflow with dependency management and build pipelines. Second, the time needed to rewrite all this code in JavaScript.

PHP-only registered blocks remove both these obstacles.

In 2022, I wanted to migrate a classic theme to a block theme.

The content area and the footer were straightforward to rebuild with blocks. But the header was more complex, especially with the more limited block building features of the time.

So, rather than spending time rebuilding the header, I took the existing PHP-header, and wrapped it in a server-side rendered block.

That said, we need to be realistic. This header block was far from perfect. The block preview was not responsive, dropdowns didn’t work in the editor, and you could not edit anything.

Did it matter? Not at all. The block rendered perfectly on the front end, and the editor preview was good enough. And because of this approach, I could migrate the theme in hours instead of days.

Before PHP-only registration, building such blocks still required a solid JavaScript proficiency and build tooling. But now any PHP developer can use this migration path using the skills they already have.

PHP-only registered blocks are ideal for converting:

The blocks you create do not need to be perfect in the editor. What counts is that they render correctly on the front end. By using existing PHP code, adaptations to block themes will be minimal.

Here are a few things I’ve learned along the way as I’ve been playing with blocks registered with PHP.

There might be cases in which you want to have a different block rendering depending on whether the block is displayed in the admin, or on the front end.

Using the is_admin() function for this use case does not work, as it does not evaluate to true when the REST API endpoint generates the markup for the block editor preview.

But there is another function that we can use: wp_is_rest_endpoint(). If it returns true, it means that WordPress is generating a REST API endpoint request. But this could be any endpoint rendering posts, so we need to ensure that we’re dealing with the Block Renderer endpoint.

This shows different text and styling depending on whether the block is rendered in the editor or on the front end:

We’ve seen that WordPress out of the box does not give you access to the ID of the edited post in PHP-only registered blocks. There is a workaround though.

WordPress registers blocks in the init hook. This hook also runs on every admin page. When you edit a post, the ID of the edited post is passed as a GET argument in the URL, for example: https://css-tricks.com/wp-admin/post.php?post=5\&action=edit

This means that at the moment of the block registration, we can retrieve this ID. To pass it to the block, we use an attribute. But we do not want WordPress to add an interface element, so we set the source of the attribute to local.

This only works when editing an existing post. When a new post is created, there is no post ID passed through the URL. WordPress will create one when the post is first saved, and update the URL.

But this is done through JavaScript without triggering a new page load from the server. Meaning that the PHP won’t have an opportunity to access the post ID until a full page reload is done.

So, yeah, not the greatest approach. But it’s good enough to unblock you until WordPress Core adds a proper implementation to pass post data to PHP-only registered blocks.

There are situations in which it is difficult to achieve a decent preview in the editor. In certain situations, it’s even impossible.

Think, for example, of a newsletter form provided as a snippet of HTML and JavaScript. Due to the limitations we’ve seen, the editor preview will always look broken.

In a situation like this, you can implement a placeholder in the editor. This is a strategy that WordPress Core uses as well, as we can see for the Post Content block:

Users do not expect an exact preview in every case. Choose the best compromise between the time needed to achieve a proper block editor preview and the expected UX gain.

You can use WordPress optimized stylesheet enqueuing, which only enqueues stylesheets on the front end for the blocks present on that specific page.

The register_block_type function offers two arguments:

To add a CSS stylesheet, register it using wp_register_style() Then use the handle during block registration:

WordPress auto-generates a .wp-block-{namespace}-{block-name} class and adds it to the wrapper container of your block as part of get_block_wrapper_attributes().

If you need to add additional classes or styles, you can pass these to get_block_wrapper_attributes() in the render callback function.

It’s the best practice to use this class as the common root class for writing targeted styles. I prefer to use the Block, Element, Modifier (BEM) approach for writing block styles. It prevents my styles from clashing with styles provided by WordPress Core or other code.

A common scenario is that you will have existing CSS, and restructuring this code and the markup using BEM would be too much work. In that case I recommend using a unique prefix for these legacy classes.

If you are dealing with a website that uses a front-end framework like Bootstrap, avoid enqueuing any framework stylesheets. You need to only migrate the CSS instructions that the block needs, applying unique prefixes as described above.

There are two ways for WordPress to integrate the post editor into the admin:

WordPress started with the first approach but quickly realized that it made styling the block editor very difficult. Without an iframe, any admin styles can interfere with that styles of the block editor, including your custom blocks.

In practice, this means that your blocks can look different in the editor than they do on the front end. For simplicity you want to use the same styles across both the front end and the editor preview with minimal adjustment. And the iframed post editor allows you to do that.

As of WordPress 7.0, the post editor is iframed if all blocks in the post are Version 3 or higher. WordPress 7.1 will enforce the iframe approach independently of the blocks.

So, to simplify building blocks and prepare for the next release, I think it’s best to ensure that all blocks on your sites use the Block API Version 3.

JavaScript support for PHP-only registered blocks is limited to the front end. To add a script, you can register it, and then pass the handle to the view_script during registration:

WordPress will only enqueue this script when the block is present on the current page.

PHP-only registered blocks can use the Block Supports API, which allows opt-in to core features. Depending on the feature, the block editor will expose additional interface elements to the user. It will also add attributes to the block to store the user’s choices.

There are features that will work independently of the theme. Others need to be enabled by the theme through its theme.json file.

Here is an example enabling color customization for the text and background color:

WordPress will take care of the outputting the corresponding CSS classes and inline styles using get_block_wrapper_attributes().

Allowing users to customize the appearance is a good demonstration, but not something that you are likely to often use. So, let’s have a look at three useful options for PHP-only registered blocks.

All register blocks appear in the inserter by default. But this does not make sense for every block. Imagine, for example, that you use a block to migrate a legacy PHP feature only used in a single template.

In this scenario, you could set inserter to false to hide the block from the inserter. Hidden blocks stay fully functional.

Setting multiple to false allows the block to only be inserted once into each post. An example is the core More block.

Once a non-multiple block is inserted, the block’s icon is disabled in the inserter to prevent inserting a second instance.

Setting align to true enables all available alignment options:

The text alignments like left, center, and right are always available. Wide and full-width alignment are only enabled if the theme supports it.

WordPress handles outputting the necessary classes for the block’s design to reflect the desired alignment.

If you want to selectively enable alignments, you can specify them. The available options are left, center, right, wide, and full.

With these tips you should be able to make the most out of PHP-only registered blocks, even with the limitations in WordPress 7.0.

Remember the opening question: Was it worth waiting seven-and-a-half years for this?

For building new, feature-rich blocks, the answer is no. You need JavaScript to deliver the kinds of interactive and native-feeling editing experiences that WordPress users expect. PHP-only block registration won’t replace JavaScript-powered blocks, and nor should it.

Because it’s not what this feature is for.

PHP-only registered blocks are the solution for thousands of WordPress sites stuck with classic themes because of the high learning curve and high cost of rebuilding with JavaScript.

You can now take shortcodes, widgets, and template parts and port them to the block editor with the PHP skills you already have. No JavaScript. No build pipeline. No code duplication.

And these blocks that you build do not need to be perfect. As long as you can insert them into block content, and they render correctly on the front end, that is all that is needed.

That is the killer use case for this feature. And for that, the wait was worth it.

But beyond this feature, PHP-only registered blocks signal an important shift: WordPress Core is finally prioritizing developer experience. Even as someone who builds JavaScript-powered blocks regularly, I’ll admit that the process involves too much boilerplate code, and too much coordination between block.json, the PHP code, and the JavaScript. Which is not to mention that time spent setting up and maintaining the build pipeline.

Anything that we can do to make this process easier, or avoid it entirely, is more than welcome.

So if you have projects with legacy PHP code preventing a migration to a block theme, then WordPress 7.0 has removed your biggest obstacle.

Migrate these legacy features to blocks and unlock everything modern WordPress has to offer.
